messages.subject_clean: about colors in plot
messages.body_plain:
Do you have an example?

You should set your point color as either colour = "green" or color = "green". I usually use the Commonwealth spelling because Hadley is a Kiwi.
If you simply want to color a layer of points "green", then put the color attribute outside of aes().
Like so:
ggplot(data = data) +
geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), colour = "green")

If you have a factor that you can color your points by then it's:
ggplot(data = data) +
geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, colour = colorfactor))

messages.subject_clean: Unexpected results with bar_plot() and facet_wrap()
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am using ggplot2 to prepare some plots, and I noticed some errors when using geom_bar() with facet_wrap().

I attached the file "example.list" if you want to reproduce the problem.

R

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

df <- read.table("example.list",h=F)
head(df)

ggplot(df, aes(factor(df$V1)))+geom_bar()+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("boat","bike","car"))+facet_wrap(~ V2, ncol =1, scales ="free_y")
ggsave("plots_facet_wrap.pdf")

=> This will produce a plot with problem, because I should have 28 yellow boats, bu the plot clearly shows below 25.

If I produce three separate plots by separating the colours, everything works fine:

green_type  <- subset(df, df$V2 == "green")
red_type    <- subset(df, df$V2 == "red")
yellow_type <- subset(df, df$V2 == "yellow")

p1 <- ggplot(green_type, aes(factor(green_type$V1)))  +geom_bar()+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("boat","bike","car"))
p2 <- ggplot(red_type, aes(factor(red_type$V1)))      +geom_bar()+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("boat","bike","car"))
p3 <- ggplot(yellow_type, aes(factor(yellow_type$V1)))+geom_bar()+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("boat","bike","car"))

pdf("plots_no_facet_wrap.pdf")
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol=1)
dev.off()

=> 28 yellow boats in the plot, as expected.

Any idea of what is wrong here? Is it my fault or a bug in ggplot2?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> Any idea of what is wrong here? Is it my fault or a bug in ggplot2?

It seems to be to do with the factor(df$V1).

Either of these work for me (number of yellow boats look right and they
are ordered
boat, bike, car on the x-axis as per your example):

ggplot(df,aes(x=V1))+geom_bar()+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("boat","bike","car"))+facet_wrap(~V2,ncol=1,scales="free_y")

ggplot(df,aes(x=factor(V1,levels=c("boat","bike","car"))))+geom_bar()+facet_wrap(~V2,ncol=1,scales="free_y")

So don't specify the "df$" in the factor call. It is redundant having
told ggplot that
your data are in df already. I don't know what impact this is then
having, maybe ggplot
is working with an internal (in some way reordered) copy of df and your
specification of
df$V1 is then wrongly addressing this back to the original. Somebody
else can probably
clarify what is going on there.

Ron.

I was trying to insert the character string to the right side of each of the plot lines. It seems that my geom_text needs to be fixed (y-value, x-value, and hjust in the geom_text).

p <- ggplot(data, aes(x=xcovariate_f, or,y=or, ymin=lc, ymax=uc))+

             scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,4.25))

Using uc to set the y coordinate is what you need to do if you want the
labels just to the right

looks very nice, so if you want

coordinate appropriately, eg:

p+geom_text(aes(label=string.est,y=max(uc)+0.1),hjust=-0.02,colour="black",size=3)+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,4.25))

The other things are just tweaks to adjust positions and size of the
text and to make
enough room in the plot for the labels.

You will want to play with the values a bit.

Ron.

messages.subject_clean: legend.key versus geom_smooth (ggplot2 1.0.0)
messages.body_plain:
Dear folks,

I've been using ggplot2 for a while now, and gotten some really good plots from it.  It's my default choice now, so thanks to all, especially Hadley!

But... you knew this was coming... one little thing that I can't seem to get right.  My colleagues have asked for plots with a white background (and the journal will also ask for this) so I'm using "theme_bw()" as in the following snippet:

---------------------
df <- data.frame(c(1:10,1:10),runif(20,-2,2),c(rep("alpha",times=10),rep("beta",times=10)))
colnames(df) <- c("x","y","tag")
x <- ggplot(df,aes(x=x,y=y,color=tag)) +
             geom_smooth(method="loess") +
             theme_bw()
print(x)
---------------------

but the background of the legend keys is still grey (see attached "sample_bw.pdf").  If I add "theme(legend.key = element_rect(fill="transparent"))" as in:

---------------------
x = ggplot(df,aes(x=x,y=y,color=tag)) +
             geom_smooth(method="loess") +
             theme_bw() +
             theme(legend.key = element_rect(fill="transparent"))
----------------------

then the background of the keys remains grey (see "sample_transparent.pdf").  Likewise if I set it to white (but it turns blue if I set it to "blue"...).  But... if I replace "geom_smooth" with "geom_line", then it behaves as expected (see attached "sample_line.pdf"):

---------------------
x = ggplot(df,aes(x=x,y=y,color=tag)) +
             geom_line() +
             theme_bw() +
             theme(legend.key = element_rect(fill="transparent"))
----------------------

So... what is it about "geom_smooth" that won't allow a transparent or white background for the keys, but will allow blue???  Can somebody tell me how to set the background of the key to white (or transparent) while still using "geom_smooth"?  I've tried various things, up to and including re-defining "theme_bw" manually, setting "legend.key" explicitly in the theme... no joy.  Any advice/help would be appreciated.

Many thanks...

Thanks for the image. Note that since you (again) didn't take the
trouble to provide a reproducible example or sample data, the
impression you're sending is that you expect people on this list to do
all your work for you. Which is not a great way to get help. However,
because I happened to have some time this morning, here's something to
get you started--hope it is useful.

library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())

# Create sample data
df <- data.frame(obs=1:20,group=LETTERS[1:10], shading=1:2,
known=c(rep(T,10),rep(F,10)),score=runif(20))

# Set up the basic plot
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=group, y=score))
p <- p + geom_blank() # not sure why I get an error without including this this

# Add background shading, alternating between groups
p <- p + geom_rect(aes(xmin=as.numeric(group)-0.5,xmax=as.numeric(group)+0.5,ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf,fill=factor(shading)),
alpha=0.2)

# Add the points
p <- p + geom_point(aes(color=known))

# Fine-tune: custom colors, horizontal line, etc.
p <- p + scale_fill_grey(guide=F)
p <- p + scale_color_manual("", values=c("green", "yellow"))  # point colors
p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept=0.5)

# Display and save the figure
print(p)
ggsave("sample.pdf")

messages.subject_clean: ggplot title
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This is one of those cases where the answer is: it's not as simple as it looks.

When you mix text and mathematical notation in R, you need to use
plotmath; see ?plotmath for an overview. Plotmath contains a number of
symbols and operators, but it also has support for "non-standard"
characters in octal or Unicode representations.

When you need to use plotmath, you typically need to create an
expression. This gets a little trickier in ggplot2 because some
functions allow you to parse character strings into plotmath
expressions (e.g., geom_text() and annotate()), whereas in other
applications you need to pass an expression, such as in axis labels
and plot titles. Therefore, the first thing you need to add to your
ggtitle code is the wrapper expression().

Next, plotmath's version of >= is a binary operator, which requires
something both to the left and right of it. Since you only want the
right hand side to show, you can stick a phantom character to the left
of the operator. The following code illustrates this approach.

DF <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
   ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*phantom("") >= 18~"Years)"))

Note: the * operator separates the string on the left from that on the
right; it is useful when you want to connect two distinct parts of the
expression without a space between them. The operator ~ inserts a
single space between the two parts to its left and right.

The operator approach is a bit clunky and only works for a single >=,
so another approach is to insert a symbol into the expression. The
symbol() function lets you insert a symbol through its octal code. The
>= symbol has octal code 263 in PDF, so the following is an
alternative to the above:

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
   ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\263")*" 18 Years)"))

The Unicode representation of the greater-than or equal to symbol is U+2265:
http://www.fileformat.info/info/unicode/char/2a7e/index.htm
Both calls below generate an equals sign in my locale:

sessionInfo()$locale
[1] "English_United States.1252"  <snipped for brevity>

#---------
ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
   ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\u2265")*" 18 Years)"))

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
   ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder (\u2265 18 Years)"))
#-------

You may or may not have better luck in a different locale. I had the
same problem when substituting the Unicode character Brandon suggested
earlier, which is the simplest way to do it

If you're in a locale where Brandon's symbol substitution works, the
other two will probably work as well, but Brandon's approach is
simpler and more understandable, particularly for single symbols.

Dennis

Hi:

Brandon's suggestion of \n will work, but when I suggested the same in
a post a couple of years ago it was pointed out that the effect of \n
is dependent on the font size (bigger font, bigger space). An
alternative is the vjust argument
in the plot.title argument of the theming system. Below, I jacked up
vjust to 3, but if you go beyond that, the title goes off the page, so
the fix in that case is to mess around with the plot.margin theme
element if you *really* want that much space between the title and the
plot region box.

The default value of vjust is 0.5. If you increase its value, text
will get pushed upward on horizontal axes or to the left on vertical
axes; if you lower it, text will be pushed downward on horizontal axes
and to the right on vertical axes. To illustrate this, I decreased the
value of vjust in axis.title.x to push the title downward, away from
the x-axis.

library(ggplot2)

DF <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = rnorm(5))

g <- ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()

g + ggtitle("ABC") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90, hjust=1, vjust=0.3),
           plot.title = element_text(size=14, face="bold", vjust = 3),
           axis.title.x = element_text(face="bold", vjust=0, size=12),
           axis.title.y = element_text(face="bold", vjust=1, size=12))

> Hi:
>
> This is one of those cases where the answer is: it's not as simple as it
> looks.
>
> When you mix text and mathematical notation in R, you need to use
> plotmath; see ?plotmath for an overview. Plotmath contains a number of
> symbols and operators, but it also has support for "non-standard"
> characters in octal or Unicode representations.
>
> When you need to use plotmath, you typically need to create an
> expression. This gets a little trickier in ggplot2 because some
> functions allow you to parse character strings into plotmath
> expressions (e.g., geom_text() and annotate()), whereas in other
> applications you need to pass an expression, such as in axis labels
> and plot titles. Therefore, the first thing you need to add to your
> ggtitle code is the wrapper expression().
>
> Next, plotmath's version of >= is a binary operator, which requires
> something both to the left and right of it. Since you only want the
> right hand side to show, you can stick a phantom character to the left
> of the operator. The following code illustrates this approach.
>
> DF <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5)
> library(ggplot2)
>
> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*phantom("") >= 18~"Years)"))
>
> Note: the * operator separates the string on the left from that on the
> right; it is useful when you want to connect two distinct parts of the
> expression without a space between them. The operator ~ inserts a
> single space between the two parts to its left and right.
>
> The operator approach is a bit clunky and only works for a single >=,
> so another approach is to insert a symbol into the expression. The
> symbol() function lets you insert a symbol through its octal code. The
>>= symbol has octal code 263 in PDF, so the following is an
> alternative to the above:
>
> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\263")*" 18 Years)"))
>
> The Unicode representation of the greater-than or equal to symbol is
> U+2265:
> http://www.fileformat.info/info/unicode/char/2a7e/index.htm
> Both calls below generate an equals sign in my locale:
>
> sessionInfo()$locale

>
> #---------
> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\u2265")*" 18 Years)"))
>
> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder (\u2265 18 Years)"))
> #-------
>
> You may or may not have better luck in a different locale. I had the
> same problem when substituting the Unicode character Brandon suggested
> earlier, which is the simplest way to do it
>
> If you're in a locale where Brandon's symbol substitution works, the
> other two will probably work as well, but Brandon's approach is
> simpler and more understandable, particularly for single symbols.
>
> Dennis

>> right hand side to show, you can stick a phantom character to the left
>> of the operator. The following code illustrates this approach.
>>
>> DF <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5)
>> library(ggplot2)
>>
>> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*phantom("") >= 18~"Years)"))
>>
>> Note: the * operator separates the string on the left from that on the
>> right; it is useful when you want to connect two distinct parts of the
>> expression without a space between them. The operator ~ inserts a
>> single space between the two parts to its left and right.
>>
>> The operator approach is a bit clunky and only works for a single >=,
>> so another approach is to insert a symbol into the expression. The
>> symbol() function lets you insert a symbol through its octal code. The
>>>= symbol has octal code 263 in PDF, so the following is an
>> alternative to the above:
>>
>> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\263")*" 18 Years)"))
>>
>> The Unicode representation of the greater-than or equal to symbol is
>> U+2265:
>> http://www.fileformat.info/info/unicode/char/2a7e/index.htm

>>

>>
>> #---------

>>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder ("*symbol("\u2265")*" 18 Years)"))
>>
>> ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
>>    ggtitle(expression("Tx by Yr\nOlder (\u2265 18 Years)"))
>> #-------
>>
>> You may or may not have better luck in a different locale. I had the
>> same problem when substituting the Unicode character Brandon suggested
>> earlier, which is the simplest way to do it
>>
>> If you're in a locale where Brandon's symbol substitution works, the

Hi Samuel,
I'm not clear what your data is or how much you have, but perhaps you might like to plot age on the X-axis and circumference on the Y-axis and then join up the data on each tree with a line and have everything on one plot?

qplot(age, circumference, data=Orange, colour=Tree, geom='path')
or something like that - assuming that the data is ordered by age...
i.e. Orange <- Orange[order(Orange$age),]
This of course will get quite messy if you have a lot of trees

Alternatively you could put each tree on a separate plot using faceting... as long as you don't have too many trees!
qplot(age, circumference, data=Orange, geom='path') + facet_wrap(~Tree)

If you have a lot of trees you might consider grouping them into tens...
Orange$TreeGroup <- Orange$Tree %/% 10
Orange$TreeNo <- Orange$Tree %% 10

qplot(age, circumference, data=Orange, colour=TreeNo, geom='path') + facet_wrap(~TreeGroup)

Lots of possibilities to play with!

Kind regards,

Hi:

ggplot() requires data frame input, so the question is whether
nlme::Orange is a data frame:

> str(Orange)
Classes ‘nfnGroupedData’, ‘nfGroupedData’, ‘groupedData’ and
'data.frame':      35 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ Tree         : Ord.factor w/ 5 levels "3"<"1"<"5"<"2"<..: 2 2 2 2 2
2 2 4 4 4 ...
 $ age          : num  118 484 664 1004 1231 ...
 $ circumference: num  30 58 87 115 120 142 145 33 69 111 ...
 - attr(*, "formula")=Class 'formula' length 3 circumference ~ age | Tree
  .. ..- attr(*, ".Environment")=<environment: R_EmptyEnv>
 - attr(*, "labels")=List of 2
  ..$ x: chr "Time since December 31, 1968"
  ..$ y: chr "Trunk circumference"
 - attr(*, "units")=List of 2
  ..$ x: chr "(days)"
  ..$ y: chr "(mm)"

We see that it is. The 'groupedData' class, as far as ggplot2 is
concerned, is simply a data frame with several additional attributes.
This can be seen as follows:

> orange <- as.data.frame(Orange)
> str(orange)
'data.frame':   35 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ Tree         : Ord.factor w/ 5 levels "3"<"1"<"5"<"2"<..: 2 2 2 2 2
2 2 4 4 4 ...
 $ age          : num  118 484 664 1004 1231 ...
 $ circumference: num  30 58 87 115 120 142 145 33 69 111 ...

Either form will work with ggplot2. Since the Orange data is about
growth curves, let's plot some:

library(ggplot2, quietly = TRUE)

# To plot the growth curves for each tree, we need
# to use the group aesthetic:
ggplot(Orange, aes(x = age, y = circumference, group = Tree)) +
   geom_line(size = 1) +
   geom_point()

# To get separate colors for each line, one way is
last_plot() + aes(color = Tree)

The ordering of the tree numbers in the legend comes from the fact
that Tree is an ordered factor.

Dennis

Hi:

The fill aesthetic in geom_point() only works for a few point shapes
(21-25), but it wouldn't change the result in the legend. This is not
exactly what you asked for, but one alternative is to increase the
point size in the legend, which you can do using guide_legend().
Extending your example,

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length,y=Petal.Length, colour=Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5)))

task, although it may be possible with some combination of gtable and
grid graphics.

messages.body_plain:
If you sort the data by z within levels of x and define a new
'ordered' y variable prior to the ggplot() call, you can get what I
believe you want:

library(plyr)
dat2 <- arrange(dat1, x, z)
dat2$y1 <- factor(seq(20))

ggplot(dat2, aes(x = x, y = y1, fill = z)) + geom_tile() +
   scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("black", "white"))

Dennis
